ai.claude: Privacy is the real product here: a camera on your face is useful only if people around you tolerate it. For site work, hands-free questions about what you are looking at (a detail, a label, a defect) are a more practical use than social video, but only once companies allow such cameras on site.
ai.fact: Google opened pre-orders for its first Gemini-powered smart glasses, built with Samsung and sold in Warby Parker and Gentle Monster frames. They have a 12MP camera, open-ear speakers and up to nine hours of battery, but no display; Google says faces of bystanders are blurred before Gemini sees them. Sales start on 10 December in the US and South Korea, against Meta, which shipped 81% of AI glasses in the first half of the year.

austrian.claude: In Austrian terms this is a shift in time preference: holders with short horizons hand coins to holders with long ones. But 'fear is a buy signal' only works in hindsight; with US 10-year yields above 5% and the AI trade wobbling, Bitcoin is still trading as a risk asset, and cheap can get cheaper.
austrian.fact: Bitcoin traded around $69,000 at midday, down about 9% on the week. On-chain data show more than $680 million of realised losses on Thursday.

opinion.text: argues that the sellers are mostly late buyers who bought above $80,000 and now sell at prices they once wished to buy; fear this deep has historically marked better entry points than exits.

mainstream.claude: Switzerland is the counter-example both sides quote: it has taxed net wealth in every canton for decades, but at low rates and with no capital-gains tax on private shares. The Dutch fight is less about whether to tax wealth than about how high and how it is valued.
mainstream.fact: Prime Minister Rob Jetten's party passed a wealth-tax bill by a narrow margin with opposition votes, and a centre-right coalition partner threatened to quit. It comes a week after California voters rejected a tax on billionaires.

opinion.text: Wealth taxes penalise saving and investment; taxing the sources of wealth, such as capital gains, reaches the same goals better.

thread.text: Jensen Huang resigned and CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO; Nvidia closed down 4% after a 14% intraday drop, while Anthropic's IPO is reportedly six times oversubscribed (Nvidia, Semafor).
thread.title: AI trade

top.claude: The market reaction was milder than the headlines: rivals and hyperscalers rose, and Anthropic's IPO is reportedly six times oversubscribed. That suggests investors see a governance shock at one company, not the end of AI spending. The 17 November results will show whether customers agree.
top.fact: Nvidia said Jensen Huang has stepped down as chief executive and left the board with immediate effect, and that CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a successor. The exit followed reports of several affairs, including one with a Megaspeed executive US authorities link to Chinese intelligence; Reuters reported a third relationship after the resignation. The shares closed down about 4% on Thursday after falling more than 14% during the session, while AMD rose nearly 6%. Earnings are due on 17 November.

opinion.text: Huang's exit ends the 'Nvidia put': the company was one of the AI trade's biggest buyers and backers, so the buildout gets more expensive for everyone.

top.fact: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces growing criticism from lawmakers of his own party for not sanctioning Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer accused of smuggling chips, and several Republican senators want him and Huang to testify. Singapore said the US gave only limited help with its own investigation of the Megaspeed executive. Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before Congress.

opinion.text: The affair exposes the administration's deep vulnerability on chip policy, after months of deferring to the Nvidia chief.

top.claude: Walking away without strikes or a deal is a third option few planned for. It keeps oil risk priced in and pushes Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE to negotiate their own terms with Iran.
top.fact: President Trump said on Thursday that the US does not need a deal with Iran, ending the negotiations led by his vice president and undercutting a Gulf-backed push to end the war. Earlier in the week he had also said further US strikes were not needed. The status of the Strait of Hormuz remains open and Brent is still near $96.

opinion.text: Iran will not 'cry uncle': the war has not broken Tehran, and the end of the midterms does not change that.

top.claude: Mearsheimer's case rests on demography and attrition, which are real, but it leaves out that Russia's own costs are also rising. If Starlink access is indeed a bargaining chip, it shows how much of Ukraine's defence now depends on one private US company.
top.fact: Ukraine said a fresh disruption of Starlink services hampered military operations, and suggested it could be US pressure in the negotiations. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Vladimir Putin in Moscow after three-way talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week produced no breakthrough. Tankers carrying Russian diesel to the US turned back for lack of buyers.

opinion.text: Ukraine cannot win, and European leaders who keep it fighting are pursuing a morally and strategically bankrupt policy.

top.claude: Mexico has already given Washington most of what it asked for on the border, so a tariff threat now looks aimed at a domestic audience after the Democrats' midterm gains. Doubling tariffs would also hit US car and food supply chains.
top.fact: President Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico unless it stops a migrant caravan heading for the US border. Illegal crossings have fallen sharply in his second term, partly because Mexico, which sends most of its exports to the US, deployed troops to stop them. Trump recently made Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, his chief of staff.

top.claude: Washington's minerals deals give it little reason to object, which is exactly why the opposition fears the decree will stand.
top.fact: Félix Tshisekedi signed a decree that could let him run for a third term, which opponents call an attempt to cling to power. Under him the DRC has moved closer to Washington: US imports from the country have risen more than a hundredfold, led by tin, and foreign investment is at a record. Corruption is widespread, militias still hold large areas, and an Ebola epidemic has killed thousands despite more than $1 billion in donor money.
